### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A27 and A33 averaged about 0.88 hours (median 0.87, middle half 0.78–0.96) over 35 observed intervals; in the later window it averaged about 0.47 hours (median 0.48, middle half 0.42–0.53) over 54 intervals — a drop of about 0.41 hours, roughly half, and fewer than 1 in 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data produced a difference this large. [TWAIT001]
- The elapsed time from A34 to A33 fell from about 0.20 hours on average (median 0.15, middle half 0.06–0.29, 54 intervals) to about 0.08 hours (median 0.07, middle half 0.03–0.12, 48 intervals), again with fewer than 1 in 1000 random re-splits matching the difference. [TWAIT002]
- Both flagged transitions end at A33 and both show shorter, less spread-out intervals in the later window (for A27→A33 the spread shrank from about 0.11 to 0.07 hours standard deviation). [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]
- Screening flagged two timing items where about 0.02 would be expected by chance, and no control-flow items (0 against about 0.28 expected). [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a timing change around A33: in the later window, the elapsed time from the completion of A27 to the completion of A33 is roughly half of what it was (about 0.88 vs 0.47 hours on average), and the elapsed time from A34 to A33 fell to under half (about 0.20 vs 0.08 hours). Supporting signs: both transitions into A33 move in the same direction, each difference exceeds about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits, the time family produced 2 items against roughly 0.02 expected without a change, and the control-flow family produced none, so the difference appears to be in timing rather than structure. Limitations: TWAIT measures elapsed time between consecutive completion events, so the shorter intervals cannot be split into waiting versus processing time, and because both items end at A33 they may reflect one underlying change at or immediately before A33 rather than two independent shifts. A competing explanation the evidence cannot fully rule out is finite-sample variation between the two 200-trace windows, although the empirical strength of both items makes a purely chance difference unlikely. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Other differences: the number of observed A27→A33 consecutive completion pairs rose from 35 to 54, while A34→A33 pairs fell slightly from 54 to 48; with no control-flow items qualifying, this frequency shift may be sampling variation and is not part of the main hypothesis. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]
